name: Facial toning

card.summary: Facial exercise routines that work the muscles of the face, jaw and neck, used in the hope of a fuller, more defined and lifted look.
card.note: Dermatologists say repeated exaggerated expressions may deepen lines.

quick.overview:
Facial toning means exercises that work the muscles of the face, jaw and neck. People do them hoping for fuller cheeks, a more defined and lifted look, and a younger appearance, without surgery or injectables. The term is listed alongside mewing as a related non-surgical practice.

A small 2018 Northwestern trial of 32 facial exercises in middle-aged women reported fuller cheeks and a lower estimated apparent age after 20 weeks.
quick.how: In the Northwestern study, participants had two 90-minute training sessions, then did 30 minutes of exercises daily for 8 weeks and every other day for the next 12. Other routines vary widely.
quick.risks: Dermatologists describe the exercises as harmless for most people, but say repeated exaggerated movements may deepen wrinkles over time and that strengthening muscle does not restore lost collagen and fat.

lead: Facial toning is the practice of exercising the muscles of the face, jaw and neck so the face looks fuller, more defined or lifted. It is a non-surgical approach, and Wikipedia lists it as a topic related to mewing, the tongue-posture practice that is likewise promoted for facial structure.[3]

Proponents say that, as with other muscles, regular exercise increases the tone and bulk of facial muscles and so changes how the cheeks and jaw look. A 2018 JAMA Dermatology study led by Murad Alam at Northwestern University tested this idea with a 32-exercise program and reported higher cheek fullness and a lower apparent age at 20 weeks.[1]

Dermatologists commenting on the practice describe the exercises as harmless for most people while saying they cannot rebuild the collagen, elastin and fat lost with age, and that exaggerated repeated expressions may deepen lines.[2]

chain: Repeated facial and jaw muscle exercises
Muscles of the cheeks and face become stronger and fuller
Fuller cheeks and a more lifted, defined look
angle.text: Practitioners exercise facial muscles hoping the face looks more toned. In the one published trial, blinded dermatologists rated upper and lower cheek fullness as improved and estimated participants as younger.

paras: Facial toning covers varied exercise routines performed to change how the face looks, including cheek-lifting, jaw and lip movements. Programs differ in content and time commitment. The goal is typically a lifted, fuller midface and cleaner jaw and neck line, which proponents link to muscle tone.
The practice is distinct from mewing, which Wikipedia describes as oral posture training rather than a facial exercise.[3]

In the Northwestern trial, participants received two 90-minute in-person sessions with an instructor, then practiced at home for 30 minutes daily for the first 8 weeks and every other day for weeks 9 to 20. Each of the 32 exercises lasted about a minute, and examples included cheek-focused moves called the Cheek Lifter and Happy Cheeks Sculpting.[1]

A dermatology practice blog says exercises may strengthen muscle but will not reverse sagging caused by loss of collagen and fat, and that repeated exaggerated movements may deepen wrinkles, much as habitual frowning creates lines. It describes them as harmless for most people and recommends they not replace professional care.[2]

The main published study is a 2018 JAMA Dermatology trial from Northwestern University. Women aged 40 to 65 learned 32 facial exercises; 27 were recruited and 16 completed the full program. Two blinded dermatologists rated standardized photographs at baseline, week 8 and week 20. Upper and lower cheek fullness improved significantly, and estimated apparent age fell from 50.8 years at baseline to 49.6 at week 8 and 48.1 at week 20.[1]

The exercises were developed by Gary Sikorski of Happy Face Yoga, a study coauthor. The sample was small and consisted only of middle-aged women, and the authors said larger studies are needed. Lead author Alam said the result was almost a three-year decrease in apparent age over 20 weeks.[1]

timeline.event: Northwestern University researchers publish a 20-week facial exercise trial in JAMA Dermatology.[1]
